# Writing style — comments, help text, and CLI output

This file is the house style for everything a reader sees: Go doc comments,
`--help` output, and the strings a command prints or returns as errors. It
applies to every Go file in this repository. Keep it short enough that it can
be re-read before every PR.

---

## Code comments

**Explain why, not what changed.** A comment answers the question the code
cannot: the invariant, the trade-off, the reason a non-obvious choice is the
safe one. It never narrates history.

- Never reference a PR, issue, fix, or the past tense of the code itself.
  "Used to", "now", "previously", "after the refactor", "fixes #123" are all
  forbidden. Git history already knows; the reader of the code does not care.
- A doc comment on every exported symbol. One or two sentences is usually
  enough. `golint` enforces this; don't make a reviewer do it.
- Target ≤ 10 lines per doc block. If you need more, the extra content
  belongs in `docs/` or a README, not above the function.
- "Deliberately not X" comments are encouraged when they stop a plausible
  wrong refactor. `internal/gitops/remote.go` is the exemplar: it says the
  function is *not* used to derive the cache directory, and why.
- No TODO, FIXME, HACK, or XXX in committed code. File an issue instead.

---

## Help text (cobra)

`--help` is reference material, not a blog post. A reader in a terminal wants
to know what the command does, what it costs, and which flags change the
behavior. Philosophy and motivation belong in `docs/`.

- **`Short:`** one line, imperative verb, no trailing period.
  Good: `Pin a component's image digest into an environment`
  Bad:  `This command pins the image digest.`
- **`Long:`** target ≤ 150 words, hard ceiling ~200. Cover: what it does,
  what it reads, what it writes, what can go wrong that the user can prevent.
  Cut: why the command exists, why GitOps is good, architecture essays.
- **`Use:`** positional args in `<>`, optional in `[]`, variadic as `name...`.
  Good: `pin <component> [version]`
  Bad:  `pin COMPONENT [VERSION]`, `pin <component> [<version>]`

If a `Long:` draft exceeds 200 words, the excess is almost always the second
paragraph onwards. Move it to a file under `docs/` and keep the help text
to usage.

---

## Flag descriptions

Use the shared constants in `cmd/intropy/flagtext.go`. Never hand-write a new
description for a flag another command already has:

- `--output`, `--env`, `--gitops-repo`, `--argocd-server`, `--domain`,
  `--system`, `--template-version` all have constants.
- If you add a flag that several commands will share, add a constant first.
- Flag descriptions are fragments, not sentences: no trailing period, no
  "This flag…". Start with the noun. Good: `target environment (required)`.

---

## Runtime output

A CLI's output is read twice: once by a human scanning, once by a script
parsing. The two never share a stream.

- **stdout is for results.** Tables, JSON, the thing the command was run to
  produce.
- **stderr is for everything else.** Progress, warnings, completion messages,
  errors. A pipeline reading stdout must never see a status line.

### Voice

- Progress and completion: **lowercase, present tense, no trailing period**.
  Good: `syncing api on argocd.example.com at a1b2c3d`
  Good: `published ghcr.io/example/releases/api:1.2.0`
  Bad:  `Published ghcr.io/…`  `Sync complete.`

I read the release and deploy code. Here's what I found and what I'd suggest.

## Where the flaw is

Both `release create` and `deploy pin <component>` (without a version) treat **HEAD of the local checkout** as "the thing being shipped" (`internal/source/source.go:48`). HEAD answers "what did I last pull?", not "what do I want to ship?". Those match only when nobody else has pushed in between.

The plumbing to fix this is mostly already there:
- `release.Options.Ref` exists and `Create` resolves it and checks that it has been pushed (`internal/release/create.go:83`). But it's labelled an "internal test seam" and has no CLI flag.
- The changelog is computed from the previous release to the chosen commit, so it already works for any commit.
- `deploy pin <component> <version>` reads the digests from the release manifest and never looks at HEAD. That path is already correct.

## Suggestion

**1. Expose `--ref` on `release create`.** It accepts a sha, tag or branch and defaults to HEAD. The pushed-commit check stays. "Release `a1b2c3d`" becomes the normal way to release, not a workaround.

**2. Make the default smarter: the newest commit that touched the component, not HEAD.** Run `git log -1 origin/<default> -- <sourcePaths>`. These are monorepos, so the commit someone else slipped in usually touched a different component, and the right answer is your commit. It probably also fixes a hidden bug. If CI only builds components whose paths changed, there may be no `sha-<HEAD>` image for this component at all, and `--watch` would wait forever. Check whether your pipeline uses path filters.

Print the chosen commit and the commits being skipped, e.g. `releasing a1b2c3d (HEAD is 9f8e7d6; 2 newer commits don't touch api)`, so the choice is never silent.

**3. Separate the dirty-tree check from the commit choice.** Today `Inspect` always checks HEAD's working tree, even when you release another commit. It should only run when the chosen commit is HEAD. In the other cases your local edits aren't part of what ships.

**4. Make "deploy by version" the normal path beyond dev.** `deploy pin` from HEAD has the same problem. Once releasing a specific commit is easy, the flow becomes: release the commit, then deploy the version. "Deploy HEAD" stays a dev convenience.

## What this doesn't solve

If the other person's commit touches the **same** component and lands between yours and the release, no ref choice can leave it out. A release is everything up to a commit. You can release the commit just before theirs and still get yours (ancestry handles that), but releasing yours without theirs needs a revert or a release branch. I'd keep that out of scope and say so in the docs rather than build cherry-pick support.

I'd start with 1–3 as one PR, since they're small and contained in `internal/source` and `internal/release`. Want me to implement it?

content.text:
I've made the changes. Nothing is committed: 12 files are modified in the working tree. All tests pass with `go test -tags integration ./...`, and gofmt is clean. golangci-lint reports 45 issues on both `main` and this branch, so none are new.

## What changed

**What gets shipped by default** (`internal/source/source.go`)
- With no ref given, the commit is now the newest one on HEAD that touched the component's `sourcePaths`, instead of HEAD itself. A teammate's push to another component no longer changes what you release.
- The search follows only the main line of history, so if you merge with merge commits it picks the merge commit (the one CI built), not the commit on the feature branch.
- When newer commits are skipped, the CLI says so on stderr: `using a1b2c3d, the newest commit under the component's source paths; HEAD (9f8e7d6) is 2 commit(s) ahead and touches none of them`
- An unpushed local commit that only touches other components no longer blocks a release.
- With an explicit ref, the uncommitted-changes check is skipped, because local edits aren't part of a named commit. The commit must still be pushed. Annotated tags resolve to the commit they point at.

**`release create --ref <sha|tag|branch>`** (`cmd/intropy/release_create.go`)
- The new flag is wired through to `release.Options.Ref`, which is no longer marked as test-only. The duplicate ref handling in `create.go` is gone.
- Combining `--ref` with `--allow-dirty` is rejected as a usage error, the same way `deploy pin` rejects it with a version.
- The help text is updated.

**Behaviour changes to review**
- **`deploy pin <component>` without a version** uses the same `source.Inspect` code, so it gets the same smarter default and the same skipped-commits message. I didn't add `--ref` to deploy.
- **Retries:** two release manifests no longer have to agree on `Source.Ref` to count as the same release. Without that, retrying with `--ref <sha>` after a first run without `--ref` would be refused as a different release. The commit and repo must still match.
- **Recorded ref:** `Source.Ref` is still written as `"HEAD"` when no ref is given, even if an older commit was picked. Its doc comment says so.

**Smaller pieces**
- **Git helpers:** two new helpers in `internal/git/client.go`, `LastChange` and `CountFirstParent`.
- **Unpushed-commit error:** it now reads `a1b2c3d is not an ancestor of …` instead of `HEAD (…)`, since the commit may not be HEAD.

## New tests
- **Source:** newer commits outside the component are skipped, no message when HEAD is the commit, an unpushed unrelated commit doesn't block, a named ref ignores local changes, a named ref must be pushed, and an annotated tag resolves to its commit.
- **Git:** `LastChange` returns the merge commit, and `CountFirstParent` counts a merge once.
- **Release:** a teammate's commit to another component is ignored, `--ref` releases an older commit and its changelog stops there, and a retry naming the same commit by sha is recognised as the same release.
- **CLI:** `--ref` with `--allow-dirty` is rejected.

The limit from before still applies: if the teammate's commit touches the **same** component, you can release your commit by sha, but a release that includes yours and leaves out an earlier one of theirs isn't possible.
